clue.text: Historian to embrace hard drinker holding traveller up, right?

parts.note: to embrace someone is to hug them
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

indicators.note: holding says the drinker word wraps round the next pieces

parts.note: a toper is a habitual heavy drinker

indicators.note: in a down clue, up says the traveller word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a rover is a wanderer or traveller

explanation.surface: A historian is told to hug a drunk who is propping up a wanderer, and asks if that is correct.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'up' reverses the traveller; 'holding' puts that reversal plus the right letter inside the drinker. The '?' just makes the surface a query.
explanation.definitionFit: Hugh Trevor-Roper was a prominent twentieth-century British historian, Regius Professor of Modern History at Oxford.

clue.text: Rep larks around with firework

indicators.note: around says the letters of these words are moved about into a new order

explanation.surface: A salesman fools about with fireworks.
explanation.walkthrough: A rep here is a sales representative; the letters of REP LARKS are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A sparkler is a hand-held firework that throws out sparks as it burns.

clue.text: Language in good and bad odour

parts.note: a reek is a strong unpleasant smell

explanation.surface: Someone's speech is described as both pleasant and smelly.
explanation.definitionFit: Greek is the language of Greece, spoken there since antiquity.

clue.text: Revolutionary's time for a change

parts.note: the Contras were Nicaraguan rebels, so a contra is a revolutionary; the possessive supplies an S

explanation.surface: A rebel declares that the moment for change has come.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive 's gives its S as a letter here; 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A contrast is a striking difference, as in 'by way of a change', the sense the clue uses.

clue.text: Plaster for minor injuries standing firm

indicators.note: in a down clue, standing says the word is set upright, read from the bottom up

parts.note: cuts are small wounds
CO is the abbreviation for company, a firm

explanation.surface: A sticking plaster for small wounds that stays firmly in place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'standing' reverses CUTS to STUC in this down clue; 'Plaster' is the building material, not the dressing the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Stucco is a fine plaster used to coat walls or make mouldings.

clue.text: Craft's contribution to "The Dictionary of Fish"?

parts.note: a carp is a freshwater fish
a contribution to a dictionary is an entry, one headword with its definition

explanation.surface: A boat's contribution to a reference book about fish.
explanation.walkthrough: A reference book about fish would list each species as a headword; 'to The Dictionary of' only frames that reading. 'Craft' means woodwork, not a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: Carpentry is the craft of working timber; the possessive 's reads as 'is', linking it.

clue.text: 3 letter about everybody's organs

indicators.note: about says the letter wraps around the next word

parts.note: 3-down's answer is a language, so a letter of that alphabet is one like phi
everybody is all; the 's is read as 'is', adding no letter

explanation.surface: A letter written in a certain language concerning everyone's organs.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference 3 points to 3-down, the language whose alphabet includes phi.
explanation.definitionFit: Phalli is the plural of phallus, the penis or an image of it.

clue.text: The Spanish lickspittle in the fraternity's shoes

indicators.note: in says the Spanish word and the flatterer sit inside the fraternity word

parts.note: a fraternity is a brotherhood, its members brothers
el is Spanish for 'the'
a creep is a toady who fawns on superiors

explanation.surface: A Spanish sycophant is found in the footwear belonging to a college fraternity.
explanation.walkthrough: BROTHEL CREEPERS are thick crepe-soled suede shoes, popular with British Teddy boys in the 1950s.
explanation.definitionFit: Brothel creepers are a style of shoe with thick crepe soles.

clue.text: Top-ranking, high-class hairdo featured in the Mail

parts.note: U is the old British label for upper-class usage

indicators.note: featured in says the hairdo sits inside the mail word

parts.note: the post is the mail service
a perm is a permanent wave, a hairdo

explanation.surface: A posh hairstyle gets coverage in a national newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mail looks like the British newspaper but is the postal service.
explanation.definitionFit: Uppermost means highest in rank or position, the top.

clue.text: Detest taking part in rehab horror

indicators.note: taking part in says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone loathes being involved in a frightening rehabilitation clinic story.
explanation.definitionFit: To abhor is to loathe or detest something intensely.

clue.text: Return on investment by wealthy folk bearing right at junction

indicators.note: bearing says the wealthy folk carry the right letter within them

parts.note: the haves are the wealthy, as in haves and have-nots
a T-junction gives T

explanation.surface: Rich people turning right at a road junction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at' is a link placing T after the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A harvest is the yield gathered from what was sown, a return on what was invested.

clue.text: Member of feuding family given pill containing uranium

indicators.note: containing says the pill wraps around the element symbol

parts.note: a caplet is a coated, capsule-shaped tablet
U is the chemical symbol for uranium

explanation.surface: A member of a warring clan is handed a radioactive pill.
explanation.definitionFit: The Capulets are Juliet's family, at feud with the Montagues in Romeo and Juliet.

clue.text: Part of watch missing 10

indicators.note: missing says something is dropped from the watch name

parts.note: a Rolex is a luxury watch brand
X is the Roman numeral for ten

explanation.surface: A piece of a watch is lost.
explanation.walkthrough: '10' looks like a cross-reference to 10-across but is the Roman numeral X.
explanation.definitionFit: A role is an actor's part in a play or film.

clue.text: Former eastern country, catching bug, going west with eastern dressing

indicators.note: in an across clue, going west means read from right to left
catching says the country name encloses the bug word

parts.note: Siam was the former name of Thailand
to bug someone is to annoy them

explanation.surface: An old Asian kingdom, infected by a bug, sets off westward with something eastern on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'catching' puts ANNOY into SIAM as SIANNOYAM; 'going west' turns that into MAYONNAIS, then E is added.
explanation.definitionFit: Mayonnaise is a cold sauce used as a dressing for salads.

clue.text: Areas admitting no compromise in Hell

indicators.note: admitting says the underworld word lets the strict word inside

parts.note: Dis is the Roman god of the underworld, and his realm, Hell
strict rules allow no compromise

explanation.surface: Zones of Hell where no concessions are made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link here.
explanation.definitionFit: Districts are areas or regions of a country or town.

clue.text: 5 isn't interrupted by marine pest

parts.note: V is the Roman numeral for five

indicators.note: interrupted by says the marine letters break into the word

parts.note: ain't is a colloquial form of isn't
RM stands for Royal Marine

explanation.surface: Five is not disturbed by a sea pest.
explanation.walkthrough: '5' looks like a cross-reference to 5-down but is the Roman numeral V.
explanation.definitionFit: Varmint is a dialect word for a troublesome animal or person, a pest.

clue.text: Translated "braccio" as "broke"

indicators.note: translated says the word is turned into another form, its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: An Italian word for arm is rendered into English as 'broke'.
explanation.walkthrough: BORACIC is British rhyming slang: 'boracic lint' rhymes with skint, meaning penniless.
explanation.definitionFit: Boracic means penniless, from rhyming slang for skint.

clue.text: Less demure, having lots of support

definitions.meaning: more brash or brazen in manner, more brassy
read humorously as more bra-like, giving plenty of uplift

explanation.surface: A bolder outfit that is also well supported.
explanation.definitionFit: Brassier is the comparative of brassy, bold and showy; whimsically it suggests extra bra support.

clue.text: Cautious about young male cleaner

indicators.note: about says the cautious word goes round the young male

parts.note: chary means wary or cautious
a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: A wary attitude towards a young man doing the cleaning.
explanation.walkthrough: A CHARLADY is a British word for a woman paid to clean houses or offices.
explanation.definitionFit: A charlady is a cleaning woman, a char.

clue.text: It's sensible to keep books in circulation

indicators.note: to keep says the sensible word holds the books inside it

parts.note: rational means sensible and reasonable
OT is the Old Testament, a set of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: It is wise to keep library books moving around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's' is a link here; 'in circulation' is the definition, not a library notion.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotational describes going round in a circle, revolving motion like circulation.

clue.text: Lust aroused by indispensable bird

indicators.note: in a down clue, aroused means raised up, so the word is read from the bottom

parts.note: rut is the season of sexual excitement in deer, lust
key means vital or indispensable

explanation.surface: Desire is stirred by an essential bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'aroused' looks like an anagram signal but means 'raised', reversing RUT to TUR in this down clue; 'by' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A turkey is a large domesticated bird.

clue.text: Ethiop breaking rock

indicators.note: breaking says the word's letters are smashed apart and reassembled

explanation.surface: An Ethiopian breaks up rocks.
explanation.definitionFit: Ophite is a green mottled rock, a kind of serpentine.

clue.text: University locksmith

definitions.meaning: an Ivy League institution in New Haven, Connecticut
Linus ..., the American who invented the cylinder lock

explanation.definitionFit: Yale is both a US university and the lock maker whose name became a lock type.

clue.text: Black host is bonkers

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
a host is a large number, especially an army

explanation.surface: A dark-clad party host has gone mad.
explanation.walkthrough: BARMY is British slang for crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Barmy is British slang for mad, crazy, bonkers.

clue.text: Swimmer being boneheaded about river

indicators.note: about says the stupid word goes round the river letter

parts.note: oafish means stupid, boneheaded

explanation.surface: A swimmer is being stupid near the river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being' is a link; the swimmer is a fish, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: The oarfish is a very long, ribbon-shaped deep-sea fish, a swimmer.

clue.text: Head back to hill for a bit of seafood

annotationWithheld.why: Head back to hill for a bit of seafood (7): no parse found giving SCALLOP from 'Head back to hill' (POLL reversed gives LLOP, but no reading of 'hill' gives SCA)
annotationWithheld.clue: Head back to hill for a bit of seafood

clue.text: Up before the court?

parts.note: ere is an old word for before
CT is the abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: Someone appearing in front of the judges.
explanation.definitionFit: Erect means upright, standing up.

clue.text: Back-to-front anchorite with back-to-front staff for a month in revolutionary France

indicators.note: back-to-front here moves the last letter of the recluse word to the front

parts.note: an anchorite is a religious recluse, a hermit

indicators.note: this time back-to-front means the staff word is read in reverse

parts.note: a rod is a staff or stick

explanation.surface: A hermit and his staff, both turned round, mark a month in the French Revolution calendar.
explanation.walkthrough: The two 'back-to-front' work differently: the first moves HERMIT's final T to the front (THERMI); the second reverses ROD to DOR.
explanation.definitionFit: Thermidor was the eleventh month of the French Republican calendar, from July to August.
